description_full: Dollarama Inc. operates a chain of stores and provides related logistical and administrative support activities. Its stores offer general merchandise, consumables, and seasonal products. The company operates in Canada, Latin America, Colombia, Peru, Australia, and Mexico. It also sells its products through online store. The company was formerly known as Dollarama Capital Corporation and changed its name to Dollarama Inc. in September 2009. Dollarama Inc. was founded in 1992 and is headquartered in Mount Royal, Canada.

financial_summary: Dollarama, Inc. is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $41.0B market cap on $5.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 23% against a 7% cost of capital — a 16-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 45%.

The business throws off $1.0B in free cash flow — roughly 20 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.3× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 8.6×.

Shareholder yield is only 1.7%, a thin return of capital, and insiders hold 2.1% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 3.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 5% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $111 (margin of safety -38%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 30%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $78.51 to $159 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 42.5 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 24.7 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 39.0 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $175 on average, 15% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 15.6% annual cash-flow growth, 5pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 23% clears the cost of capital of 7.0% by 16pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.08).
It runs a 45% gross margin and converts 20% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.34x.
ROE of 90% is amplified by 5.2x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.

hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.3x net debt to EBITDA ($234.7M of cash against $3.8B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 8.6x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.5, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.5% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Analysts expect 13.6% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.1%, and institutions hold 47%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.7% (1.5% in buybacks and 0.2% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 12 consecutive years.
